title: Introduction to VPC
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Understand the global nature and isolation of Virtual Private Clouds in GCP.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
A Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) is a global, private network within Google Cloud. Unlike other clouds where networks are regional, a GCP VPC can span every region worldwide. This allows VMs in different countries to communicate over Google's private backbone without touching the public internet. VPCs provide logical isolation for your cloud resources.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud compute networks list` # List all VPC networks in the project
* `gcloud compute networks describe [NAME]` # Get detailed VPC configuration

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
A global enterprise uses a single VPC to connect its frontend servers in Tokyo with its backend databases in Belgium, ensuring low-latency, private communication without the need for complex VPN peering.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Assuming that because the VPC is global, the subnets are too. Subnets are always regional, even though they live inside a global VPC.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Always use a custom VPC for production to ensure you have full control over IP address allocation and avoid overlap with on-premises networks.

[SUMMARY]
VPCs are global, isolated networks that serve as the fundamental networking layer for all Google Cloud resources.
insight: Even though the VPC is global, the IP addresses (subnets) inside it are regional.

title: Default vs. Custom VPCs
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Choose the right network mode for production security and scalability.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
AUTO MODE: Automatically creates one subnet in every GCP region using a predefined range (10.128.0.0/9). This can lead to IP conflicts. CUSTOM MODE: No subnets are created automatically. You define exactly which regions need subnets and specify their CIDR ranges. Custom mode is the gold standard for production environments.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud compute networks create [NAME] --subnet-mode=custom` # Create a custom VPC
* `gcloud compute networks list` # View subnet modes of all networks

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
A security architect mandates Custom Mode VPCs for all projects to ensure that 'Dev' and 'Prod' environments have strictly segregated IP ranges that never overlap with the office VPN.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Using Auto Mode for projects that will eventually need to peer with other networks, only to find that the default IP ranges conflict with the other side.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Always convert your networks to Custom Mode at the start of a project. You can convert Auto to Custom, but you can NEVER convert Custom back to Auto.

[SUMMARY]
Custom Mode VPCs provide the granular control over IP addresses required for enterprise-grade cloud networking.
insight: On the ACE exam: Always recommend Custom Mode for production environments to avoid IP overlap.

title: Creating Regional Subnets
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Provision IP ranges within specific geographic regions for resource placement.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
In a Custom VPC, you must manually create subnets. Each subnet is tied to a specific Region (e.g., us-central1). You define the range using CIDR notation (e.g., 10.0.1.0/24). Subnets also support 'Alias IPs', which are secondary ranges used by services like GKE to give every container its own VPC IP.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud compute networks subnets create [NAME] --network=[VPC] --region=[REGION] --range=[CIDR]` # Create a subnet
* `gcloud compute networks subnets list --network=[VPC]` # List subnets in a network

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
An infrastructure team creates a `10.0.1.0/24` subnet in `us-east1` for web servers and a `10.0.2.0/24` subnet in `us-west1` for backup servers to ensure regional redundancy.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Attempting to create overlapping CIDR ranges within the same VPC, which the GCP API will block.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Plan your CIDR ranges carefully and account for the 4 reserved IP addresses Google takes from every subnet (Network, Gateway, Reserved, Broadcast).

[SUMMARY]
Subnets are regional resources that define the internal IP structure of your global VPC network.
insight: GCP reserves 4 IP addresses in every subnet (Network, Gateway, Reserved, Broadcast). Plan your range size accordingly!

title: VPC Firewall Fundamentals
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Secure your network using stateful, distributed firewall rules.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
GCP firewalls are 'distributed'—they are enforced at the individual VM level, not at the network gateway. They are STATEFUL: if you allow an inbound (ingress) request, the response (egress) is automatically allowed. Every VPC has an 'Implicit Deny Ingress' that blocks all incoming traffic by default.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud compute firewall-rules list` # View all firewall rules
* `gcloud compute firewall-rules create [NAME] --allow=[PROTOCOL:PORT] --direction=INGRESS` # Create a rule
* `gcloud compute firewall-rules delete [NAME]` # Remove a rule

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
A developer creates a rule to allow TCP port 22 (SSH) from their office IP, ensuring they can manage VMs while keeping the rest of the world blocked.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Thinking a firewall is a single hardware device. Because it's distributed, a misconfigured rule on one VM doesn't necessarily affect others in the same subnet.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Use rule priorities (0-65535) to resolve conflicts. Lower numbers have higher priority and are evaluated first.

[SUMMARY]
GCP firewalls provide granular, per-VM security that is integrated directly into the software-defined network.
insight: Firewall rules have a priority from 0 to 65535. Lower numbers (higher priority) win conflicts.

title: Tags vs. Service Accounts
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Identify the most secure and scalable way to target firewall rules.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
You can target firewall rules in two ways: 1. NETWORK TAGS: Simple strings (e.g., 'web-server'). Easy to use but less secure as anyone with VM modify permissions can change them. 2. SERVICE ACCOUNTS: Highly secure. Rules apply based on the VM's identity. Only an IAM Admin can change an instance's service account.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud compute firewall-rules create [NAME] --allow=tcp:80 --target-tags=web-tier` # Tag-based rule
* `gcloud compute firewall-rules create [NAME] --allow=tcp:443 --target-service-accounts=[SA_EMAIL]` # SA-based rule
* `gcloud compute instances add-tags [VM] --tags=[TAG]` # Apply a tag

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
A security-conscious organization uses Service Accounts for firewall targeting to ensure that security policies are tied to the 'Identity' of the workload, preventing 'tag spoofing'.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Using Network Tags in production environments where strong security boundaries are required. Tags are essentially 'security by label', not 'security by identity'.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Use Service Accounts for production firewall rules to ensure that a developer cannot bypass security by simply adding a tag to a VM.

[SUMMARY]
While tags are convenient for labs, Service Account-based targeting is the industry best practice for production VPC security.
insight: Network Tags are case-sensitive—watch out for 'Web-Tier' vs 'web-tier' typos!

title: Static External IPs
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Provide stable, public endpoints for your internet-facing resources.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
By default, VMs get ephemeral IPs that change on restart. A STATIC IP is reserved in your project and stays with you. There are two types: REGIONAL (for VMs and regional LBs) and GLOBAL (used ONLY for Global HTTP(S) Load Balancers).

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud compute addresses create [NAME] --region=[REGION]` # Reserve a regional static IP
* `gcloud compute addresses create [NAME] --global` # Reserve a global static IP
* `gcloud compute addresses list` # View all reserved IPs

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
A company reserves a static IP for its primary web server so it can point its `www` DNS record to a fixed address that never changes.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Reserving static IPs and not attaching them to resources. Google charges a small fee for 'unused' static IPs to prevent resource hoarding.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Only use static IPs when strictly necessary for DNS or external whitelisting; use Load Balancers for most public-facing traffic instead.

[SUMMARY]
Static IPs ensure your public services remain reachable at a consistent address, but they require careful management to avoid unnecessary costs.
insight: If you delete a VM, the attached static IP remains in your project—don't forget to delete it too!

title: Cloud DNS: Public Zones
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Manage internet-facing domain records using Google's global infrastructure.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
Cloud DNS is a highly available, managed Domain Name System. A Public Zone hosts records (A, CNAME, etc.) for domains you own. Google provides four Anycast Name Servers (NS) that you must update at your registrar to make Google the 'authoritative' DNS for your domain.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud dns managed-zones create [NAME] --dns-name=[DOMAIN]. --visibility=public` # Create public zone
* `gcloud dns managed-zones list` # View all DNS zones

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
A startup uses Cloud DNS to manage the A-records for their website, ensuring users worldwide get sub-millisecond DNS resolution speeds through Google's edge network.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Forgetting to add the trailing dot (e.g., `example.com.`) in the CLI, which is required to represent the DNS root.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Enable 'DNSSEC' on your public zones to protect your users against DNS spoofing and 'man-in-the-middle' attacks.

[SUMMARY]
Cloud DNS provides the reliability and speed needed to scale internet-facing applications globally.
insight: Always end your DNS names with a dot in the CLI (e.g., 'example.com.') to represent the DNS root.

title: Cloud DNS: Private Zones
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Implement internal service discovery within VPC networks.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
A Private Zone is only visible to specific VPCs. You can create custom names like `db.prod.internal`. This is much better than hardcoding internal IPs, as you can change a VM's IP address and simply update the DNS record without changing application code.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud dns managed-zones create [NAME] --dns-name=[INTERNAL_DOMAIN]. --visibility=private --networks=[VPC]` # Create private zone
* `gcloud dns managed-zones describe [NAME]` # See which VPCs can see the zone

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
An application team uses a private DNS zone so their web servers can always reach the database at `mysql-master.internal`, regardless of which subnet the database is moved to.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Trying to reach a private DNS name from the public internet. These records only exist and resolve 'inside' the VPC backbone.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Use a consistent naming convention for internal DNS (e.g., `[service].[env].internal`) to make it easier for developers to find resources.

[SUMMARY]
Private DNS zones are the cornerstone of stable, internal service-to-service communication in the cloud.
insight: You can peer Private DNS zones across different VPCs to share internal names.

title: VPC Network Peering
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Connect two separate VPCs for high-speed, internal IP communication.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
VPC Peering connects two networks (even in different Orgs) so resources can talk via internal IPs. It is NON-TRANSITIVE: if A is peered with B, and B with C, A cannot talk to C. Both sides must create a peering link for it to become active.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud compute networks peerings create [NAME] --network=[VPC_A] --peer-network=[VPC_B]` # Create peering
* `gcloud compute networks peerings list --network=[VPC]` # View peering status

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
A company peers its 'Security-VPC' with its 'App-VPC' so the central security scanners can reach application VMs over private IP addresses.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Attempting to peer VPCs with overlapping CIDR ranges. If both networks use `10.0.0.0/24`, the peering will fail immediately.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Always check the 'peering state' in the CLI; the connection is only established once both administrators have approved the link.

[SUMMARY]
VPC Peering provides low-latency, private connectivity between distinct networks without the overhead of a VPN.
insight: Both sides must create a peering connection for the link to become 'ACTIVE'.

title: Shared VPC (Centralized Control)
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Isolate technical service management from central network administration.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
Shared VPC allows one 'Host Project' to share its network/subnets with multiple 'Service Projects'. App developers in Service Projects can deploy VMs, but they must 'plug' them into the subnets owned and managed by the central Network Team.

[COMMANDS]
* `echo 'Manage via Shared VPC tab in the Google Cloud Console'` # (Best handled via UI/Org setup)

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
A large bank uses a Shared VPC so the 'Cybersecurity Team' can manage all firewall rules in the Host Project, while the 'Retail App Team' can manage their own VMs in their Service Project.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Thinking you can use Shared VPC without an Organization node. Folders and Organizations are required to enable this enterprise feature.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Grant the `compute.networkUser` IAM role to service project admins so they can only deploy to specific, authorized subnets.

[SUMMARY]
Shared VPC is the standard for large-scale GCP environments, providing a balance between central governance and developer agility.
insight: Shared VPC is the standard for large companies; Peering is more common for quick one-off connections.

title: Cloud VPN Overview
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Securely connect on-premises data centers to GCP using IPsec tunnels over the internet.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
Cloud VPN creates an encrypted tunnel between your office and your VPC. There are two types: CLASSIC (Legacy, static routing) and HA VPN (High Availability). HA VPN uses two tunnels and BGP for dynamic routing, providing a 99.99% SLA.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud compute vpn-gateways list` # List all VPN gateways
* `gcloud compute vpn-tunnels list` # Check status of encrypted tunnels

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
A company migrating to the cloud uses HA VPN to give their developers secure access to GCP resources from their local office desktops.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Using Classic VPN for production workloads that require high uptime. Classic VPN does not provide the same SLA or redundancy as HA VPN.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Always choose HA VPN and use BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) for dynamic route exchange to ensure your network automatically updates when subnets change.

[SUMMARY]
Cloud VPN is the fastest way to establish secure hybrid-cloud connectivity between your office and the Google Cloud backbone.
insight: Always choose HA VPN over Classic VPN to ensure you meet enterprise uptime requirements.

title: Cloud Interconnect
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Establish high-speed, physical fiber connectivity for large-scale hybrid cloud workloads.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
Cloud Interconnect is a physical cable between your network and Google's. DEDICATED: 10/100 Gbps link directly into a Google router. PARTNER: 50 Mbps - 50 Gbps link through a service provider (like Equinix). Traffic never touches the public internet.

[COMMANDS]
* `echo 'Configure via Hybrid Connectivity -> Interconnect in the Console'` # (Physical hardware setup)

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
A financial data firm uses Dedicated Interconnect to move terabytes of market data to GCP every hour with the lowest possible latency and 99.99% reliability.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Assuming Interconnect is as fast to set up as a VPN. Physical installation can take weeks or months depending on the facility.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Use Interconnect if you require more than 3 Gbps of bandwidth or have strict compliance rules that forbid traffic from crossing the public internet.

[SUMMARY]
Cloud Interconnect is the premium solution for high-performance, private, and reliable hybrid cloud connectivity.
insight: Interconnect is significantly more expensive and takes weeks/months to install compared to a 5-minute VPN setup.

title: Cloud NAT (Network Address Translation)
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Enable outbound internet access for VMs that lack public IP addresses.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
A private VM (no external IP) cannot reach the internet to download updates. Cloud NAT is a managed service that allows these VMs to send outbound traffic while remaining invisible to inbound internet connections. It requires a Cloud Router to function.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud compute routers nats create [NAME] --router=[ROUTER] --auto-allocate-nat-external-ips --nat-all-subnet-ip-ranges` # Enable NAT
* `gcloud compute routers nats list --router=[ROUTER]` # List NAT configs

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
A database server is kept strictly private (no public IP) for security, but uses Cloud NAT to securely reach the internet for weekly OS security patches.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Expecting Cloud NAT to handle 'Inbound' traffic. It is strictly 'Outbound-Only'; if you need the internet to reach your VM, you need a Load Balancer or a Static IP.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Use Cloud NAT for all backend servers to minimize your project's attack surface while maintaining necessary internet connectivity for updates.

[SUMMARY]
Cloud NAT provides a secure way for private resources to reach the internet without exposing them to public threats.
insight: A single Cloud NAT gateway can handle traffic for all subnets in a specific region.

title: Network Service Tiers
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Balance network performance and cost for your internet-facing traffic.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
PREMIUM TIER (Default): Traffic enters Google's high-speed fiber backbone at the edge location closest to the user. Lowest latency. STANDARD TIER: Traffic stays on the public internet as long as possible, only entering Google's network at the destination region. Lower cost.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud compute addresses create [NAME] --network-tier=STANDARD --region=[REGION]` # Reserve Standard IP
* `gcloud compute addresses describe [NAME] --region=[REGION]` # Check tier

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
A gaming company uses Premium Tier to ensure the lowest possible 'ping' for its players, while using Standard Tier for an internal file-syncing tool where speed isn't critical.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Assuming all clouds have a 'Premium Tier' equivalent. Most other providers only offer what Google calls 'Standard Tier'.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Use Premium Tier for all customer-facing applications to ensure the best possible user experience and global availability.

[SUMMARY]
GCP's network tiers allow you to surgically choose between high-performance global transit and cost-optimized regional transit.
insight: Use Premium Tier for latency-sensitive apps (Gaming, Video); use Standard Tier for internal tools or backups.

title: Load Balancing Overview
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Select the correct load balancer based on traffic protocol and geographic scope.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
Load balancers distribute traffic across VM groups (MIGs). Key types: 1. GLOBAL HTTP(S): Layer 7, for web apps. 2. NETWORK LB: Layer 4, for raw TCP/UDP. 3. INTERNAL LB: For private, intra-VPC traffic. Load balancers are software-defined and do not need pre-warming.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud compute forwarding-rules list` # List all 'Front-end' IPs for Load Balancers

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
An e-commerce site uses a Global HTTP(S) Load Balancer to route users to the nearest regional instance group, ensuring the site stays up even if an entire region fails.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Using an External Load Balancer for traffic that stays entirely within your private VPC network. Use an Internal LB to save costs and improve security.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Always put production VMs behind a load balancer; never point your DNS records directly to a single VM's static IP.

[SUMMARY]
Load balancers are the primary mechanism for achieving scalability and high availability in Google Cloud.
insight: GCP load balancers are software-defined; they don't need to 'warm up' to handle massive traffic spikes.

title: Global HTTP(S) Load Balancing
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Route web traffic globally using a single Anycast IP and advanced L7 logic.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
This Layer 7 proxy uses one IP address for the whole world. Components: 1. Forwarding Rule (Frontend IP), 2. Target Proxy (SSL termination), 3. URL Map (Path-based logic), 4. Backend Service (VM groups/Buckets). It supports content-based routing (e.g., /api vs /images).

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud compute url-maps list` # View all L7 routing maps
* `gcloud compute backend-services list --global` # View backend VM groups

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
A global streaming app uses a single IP address. The URL Map sends traffic for `/video` to high-power VM clusters and traffic for `/static` directly to Cloud Storage buckets.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Assuming the Global LB can only route to VMs. It is the only LB that can use both VM Instance Groups and GCS Buckets as backends.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Use 'Google-managed SSL Certificates' with your Global LB to automate the creation and renewal of your HTTPS certs for free.

[SUMMARY]
The Global HTTP(S) Load Balancer is the 'Front Door' for high-traffic, global web applications.
insight: The Global LB is the only one that can route traffic to both VM groups AND Cloud Storage buckets.

title: Internal Load Balancing
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Efficiently balance traffic between private application tiers within a VPC.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
Internal Load Balancers use a private VPC IP. They are not proxies; they use Software Defined Networking (SDN) to route packets directly from client to backend. This results in extremely low latency and zero egress costs for traffic staying within the same zone.

[COMMANDS]
* `echo 'Type: INTERNAL, Protocol: TCP/UDP'` # (Configuration concept)

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
In a microservices architecture, the 'Frontend' service connects to the 'Payment' service via an Internal Load Balancer, ensuring high availability of the payment tier without exposing it to the internet.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Trying to use an Internal Load Balancer to reach resources over the public internet. These LBs are strictly for intra-VPC communication.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Use Internal LBs for all database clusters and internal API tiers to maintain a 'Zero Trust' security model where only authorized VPC resources can connect.

[SUMMARY]
Internal Load Balancers provide a high-performance, private way to scale internal services.
insight: Internal Load Balancers are free from most egress charges because traffic stays within the VPC.

title: External Network Load Balancing
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Balance non-HTTP traffic with high performance and client IP preservation.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
The Network Load Balancer is a Layer 4 regional load balancer. It handles raw TCP/UDP traffic (like SMTP or custom protocols). Unlike L7 proxies, it does not terminate SSL; it passes the packet through directly, allowing the VM to see the user's original IP address.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud compute forwarding-rules list --filter='region:us-central1'` # List regional rules
* `gcloud compute target-pools list` # View L4 backend pools

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
A VOIP company uses Network Load Balancers to handle millions of UDP packets for voice calls, where every millisecond of 'proxy overhead' would degrade call quality.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Trying to use a Network LB for path-based routing (e.g. /images). L4 load balancers only care about IP and Port; they cannot 'see' the URL path.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Use Network LB when you need to handle raw TCP/UDP traffic or when your application strictly requires the user's source IP address for logging or security.

[SUMMARY]
Network Load Balancing is the high-throughput, low-latency choice for non-web protocols.
insight: Use Network LB if you need to handle millions of requests per second with very low overhead.

title: Cloud Armor (Web Security)
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Protect your web applications from DDoS, SQL injection, and country-based threats.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
Cloud Armor is a Web Application Firewall (WAF) that integrates with the Global HTTP(S) Load Balancer. It filters traffic at Google's 'Edge', before it even enters your VPC. You can block IPs, entire countries (Geo-fencing), or use pre-defined rules to stop OWASP Top 10 attacks.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud compute security-policies create [NAME]` # Create a WAF policy
* `gcloud compute security-policies rules create [PRIORITY] --security-policy=[NAME] --src-ip-ranges=[IP] --action="deny-403"` # Block an IP

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
During a DDoS attack, a security engineer uses Cloud Armor to instantly block a list of malicious IP ranges, keeping the website alive for legitimate customers.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Assuming Cloud Armor works with Network Load Balancers. It is specifically designed to work with L7 (HTTP/S) proxies where it can inspect web traffic headers.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Enable Cloud Armor 'Managed Protection' to get automatic protection against known botnets and sophisticated application-layer attacks.

[SUMMARY]
Cloud Armor is your first line of defense against modern web-based security threats and high-volume DDoS attacks.
insight: Cloud Armor provides the same protection Google uses for Search and YouTube.

production-waf  Block OWASP Top 10

title: Cloud CDN (Caching)
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Optimize website performance and reduce egress costs using global edge caching.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
Cloud CDN caches static content (images, videos, JS) at edge locations near your users. When a user requests an image, it is served from the nearest cache rather than fetching it from your server. This reduces latency and significantly lowers your cloud bill.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud compute backend-services update [NAME] --global --enable-cdn` # Enable CDN
* `gcloud compute backend-services describe [NAME] --global --format='get(enableCDN)'` # Verify status

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
A news site uses Cloud CDN to serve its articles. Even if a story goes viral, the main web servers stay idle because 99% of users are being served by the edge cache.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Enabling CDN for dynamic content (like a user's personal profile page). Only static assets that are the same for everyone should be cached.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Set 'Cache-Control' headers in your application to tell Cloud CDN exactly how long each file should be stored (e.g. 1 hour for news, 1 year for logos).

[SUMMARY]
Cloud CDN turns Google's global edge network into a performance booster for your web application.
insight: Cloud CDN requires the use of the Global HTTP(S) Load Balancer.

title: Private Google Access
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Allow private VPC resources to reach Google APIs without using public IPs.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
Normally, a VM without a public IP cannot reach Cloud Storage or BigQuery. Private Google Access is a subnet-level setting that allows these VMs to talk to Google services over the internal backbone. No external IP or NAT gateway is required.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud compute networks subnets update [NAME] --region=[REGION] --enable-private-google-access` # Enable on subnet
* `gcloud compute networks subnets describe [NAME] --region=[REGION] --format='get(privateIpGoogleAccess)'` # Verify

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
A secure data-processing VM has no external IP to prevent hacking. It uses Private Google Access to pull 1TB of raw data from a GCS bucket for analysis over Google's private fiber.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Thinking Private Google Access lets your VM reach the general 'Internet'. It only allows access to 'Google APIs and Services'.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Always enable Private Google Access on every subnet that contains private VMs to ensure they can use essential services like Cloud Logging and Monitoring.

[SUMMARY]
Private Google Access is a simple, no-cost way to improve the security posture of your private cloud resources.
insight: On the exam: If a private VM needs to upload a file to a bucket, the best answer is 'Enable Private Google Access'.

lab.command: gcloud compute networks subnets describe default --region=us-central1 --format='get(privateIpGoogleAccess)'

title: Private Service Connect
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Consume external services privately via internal VPC endpoints.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
Private Service Connect (PSC) allows you to create an internal IP in your VPC that points directly to a service (e.g., Snowflake, MongoDB, or a Google API). Traffic is routed entirely via Google's SDN, eliminating the need for complex VPC Peering or NAT.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud compute forwarding-rules list --filter='target:all-google-apis'` # View PSC endpoints

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
A company uses PSC to connect to a third-party managed database. The database appears to the company's VMs as just another internal IP address (`10.0.0.100`) within their own VPC.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Using VPC Peering for every service connection. Peering is harder to manage and has CIDR overlap issues; PSC is cleaner and more isolated.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Use PSC for 'Service Producer' patterns where you want to provide or consume a service across different organizations securely.

[SUMMARY]
Private Service Connect is the modern, SDN-native way to bridge services across network boundaries without peering.
insight: PSC is the preferred way to consume 'Service Producer' applications securely in a large Org.

title: VPC Flow Logs (Auditing)
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Audit and troubleshoot network traffic patterns within your subnets.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
Flow Logs sample all network traffic (TCP/UDP) sent from or received by VMs. They record metadata like Source/Dest IP, Port, and Protocol. Critically, they also show if the traffic was ALLOWED or DENIED by a firewall rule.

[COMMANDS]
* `echo 'Enable in Subnet settings in the Console'` # (Best managed via UI or Subnet update)
* `gcloud compute networks subnets update [NAME] --region=[REGION] --logging-aggregation-interval=interval-5-sec` # Enable via CLI

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
An SRE team uses Flow Logs to debug why their app can't talk to a database, discovering that packets are being 'DENIED' by an egress firewall rule they forgot about.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Expecting to see the 'Payload' of the data in Flow Logs. They only record 'Metadata' (Headers). If you need the actual content, use Packet Mirroring.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Enable Flow Logs on sensitive subnets for security auditing and compliance, but use a 'sampling rate' to avoid excessive logging costs on high-traffic networks.

[SUMMARY]
VPC Flow Logs are the essential 'CCTV' for your network, providing the raw data needed for security forensic and performance debugging.
insight: Flow logs only record 'Metadata' (Headers), not the actual 'Payload' (Content) of the packets.

title: Connectivity Tests
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Simulate and debug network reachability issues without sending actual traffic.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
Connectivity Tests (part of Network Intelligence Center) allow you to simulate a packet's journey between two points. It analyzes your VPC configuration (firewalls, routes, load balancers) and tells you exactly where a packet would be dropped if it failed.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud network-management connectivity-tests list` # View recent test results
* `gcloud network-management connectivity-tests create [NAME] --source-instance=[VM_A] --destination-instance=[VM_B]` # Run simulation

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
Before a high-profile app launch, a network engineer runs a Connectivity Test between the web tier and the database tier to prove that all firewall rules and routes are correctly configured.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Manually SSHing into VMs and running `ping` or `telnet` to test connectivity. Connectivity Tests are much faster and pinpoint the *exact* rule that is blocking traffic.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Use Connectivity Tests to verify complex multi-VPC or hybrid-cloud routing where a packet might cross multiple firewalls and VPN tunnels.

[SUMMARY]
Connectivity Tests are a proactive troubleshooting tool that takes the guesswork out of network reachability debugging.
insight: Use this before a launch to verify that your complex multi-VPC routing is actually working.

title: Cloud Router & BGP
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Automate network route management for hybrid-cloud connectivity.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
Cloud Router is a managed service that uses BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) to exchange routes between your VPC and your on-prem network. It is required for HA VPN and Dedicated Interconnect. It eliminates the need to manually update static routes whenever your office network changes.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud compute routers list` # View all routers
* `gcloud compute routers describe [NAME] --region=[REGION]` # See BGP session details

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
When an IT team adds a new subnet to their office, the Cloud Router automatically 'learns' the new route via BGP and updates the GCP routing table instantly without any manual intervention.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Thinking a Cloud Router actually 'moves' packets. It is the 'Brain' that manages the routing table; the actual packet movement is handled by the VPC's underlying SDN.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Always use 'Dynamic Routing Mode: Global' in your VPC settings if you want a VPN in one region to provide access to subnets in every other GCP region.

[SUMMARY]
Cloud Router is the essential BGP management service for any enterprise building a reliable hybrid-cloud network.
insight: Cloud Router does not actually 'route' packets; it just manages the 'brain' (the routing table).

title: VPC Service Controls (Perimeters)
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Mitigate the risk of data exfiltration using security perimeters.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
VPC Service Controls allow you to define a 'Service Perimeter' around sensitive GCP services (Storage, BigQuery). It ensures that data cannot be moved outside this boundary, even by users with high-level IAM permissions. It is independent of IAM and acts as a network-level guardrail.

[COMMANDS]
* `echo 'Configure via Security -> VPC Service Controls in the Console'` # (Highly complex setup)

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
A financial institution creates a perimeter around its 'Customer-Data' project. If an administrator tries to copy a BigQuery table to their personal project, VPC Service Controls will block the request as 'Exfiltration Attempt'.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Assuming IAM is enough. IAM controls 'Who can do what', but VPC Service Controls controls 'Where data can go'. You need both for high-security environments.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Start with 'Dry-Run' mode when configuring perimeters. It will log what *would* have been blocked without actually stopping traffic, allowing you to fix errors before going live.

[SUMMARY]
VPC Service Controls provide the most robust defense against internal data leaks and external exfiltration attacks in Google Cloud.
insight: VPC Service Controls is one of the most powerful security features in GCP—and it's also the most complex to configure!

lab.command: echo 'Configure via Security -> VPC Service Controls'
lab.output: Configure via Security -> VPC Service Controls

title: Packet Mirroring (IDS/IPS)
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Perform deep packet inspection (DPI) for security and threat detection.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
Packet Mirroring clones traffic from a subnet or VM and sends it to a destination, such as an Intrusion Detection System (IDS) like Suricata. Unlike Flow Logs (metadata only), Mirroring shows the actual PAYLOAD of every packet, allowing for malware and anomaly detection.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud compute packet-mirrorings list` # View active mirroring policies
* `gcloud compute packet-mirrorings create [NAME] --network=[VPC] --mirrored-subnets=[SUB] --collector-ilb=[LB_IP]` # Start mirroring

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
A security team mirrors all traffic from the 'Payment-Processing' subnet to a cluster of analysis VMs to detect unauthorized data patterns that a firewall would ignore.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Mirroring all traffic in the entire VPC. This generates massive amounts of data and can lead to high costs. Only mirror the most sensitive subnets.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Only use Packet Mirroring when you have a specific security requirement for deep packet inspection that cannot be met by Flow Logs or Cloud Armor.

[SUMMARY]
Packet Mirroring is the ultimate visibility tool for security forensic analysis, providing a full copy of all network traffic for deep inspection.
insight: Mirroring traffic incurs extra costs for data processing and the target VMs—use it only for sensitive subnets.

title: Firewall Rules Logging
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Audit the usage of specific firewall rules for security hardening.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
You can enable logging on a per-rule basis to record every time that rule ALLOWS or DENIES a packet. This is vital for forensic investigation and for identifying 'stale' rules that haven't seen traffic in months and should be deleted.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud compute firewall-rules update [NAME] --enable-logging` # Enable logging on a rule
* `gcloud compute firewall-rules describe [NAME] --format='get(logConfig.enable)'` # Verify status

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
A security auditor enables logging on the 'Allow-All-Internal' rule to see if any legacy applications are still using unencrypted protocols that should be migrated to HTTPS.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Enabling logging on every rule in a high-traffic VPC, which can lead to a massive volume of logs and increased Cloud Logging costs.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Regularly review firewall logs to identify rules with zero hits; these are prime candidates for removal to reduce your network's attack surface.

[SUMMARY]
Firewall logging provides the granular visibility needed to maintain a clean, hardened, and secure network environment.
insight: Logging can generate a lot of data—use it selectively on important rules.
next: Standard vs Premium Tiers: Decision Guide

title: Standard vs. Premium (Deep Dive)
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Understand the physical path data packets take across the globe.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
PREMIUM TIER: Packets enter Google's network at the edge closest to the user and stay on Google's private fiber for the whole trip. STANDARD TIER: Packets stay on the messy public internet for most of the journey, only entering Google's network at the destination region.

[COMMANDS]
* `echo 'Premium = Max performance | Standard = Max cost-savings'` # (Architectural choice)

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
A video conferencing app uses Premium Tier to minimize 'jitter' and latency for global users, ensuring smooth video regardless of where the participants are located.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Thinking Standard Tier is 'bad'. It's perfectly fine for static file downloads or internal tools where a few extra milliseconds of latency don't matter.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Always check the Network Tier setting on your Static IPs; the ACE exam often tests if you know that Premium is the default but more expensive option.

[SUMMARY]
Choosing the right network tier allows you to optimize for either the lowest possible latency (Premium) or the lowest possible cost (Standard).
insight: Most other clouds only offer the equivalent of Google's 'Standard Tier' by default!

lab.command: echo 'Premium = Low Latency | Standard = Low Cost'
lab.output: Premium = Low Latency | Standard = Low Cost

title: Anycast IP (Global LB)
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Understand how Anycast technology provides global high availability with a single IP.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
Unlike standard DNS-based routing, Anycast gives you ONE IP address for the entire world. Google broadcasts this IP from every edge location. A user's packet naturally flows to the nearest physical Google router, which then passes it to the Load Balancer logic.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud compute forwarding-rules describe [FRONTEND_NAME] --global` # View the Anycast IP

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
Google Search uses Anycast. Whether you are in New York or New Delhi, you connect to the same Anycast IP range, and Google's routers automatically find the fastest path to a data center.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Assuming you need complex 'Geo-DNS' with the Global Load Balancer. Anycast handles the geographic routing automatically at the network layer.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Use a Global Static IP with your Global Load Balancer so your Anycast address never changes, even if you delete and recreate the frontend configuration.

[SUMMARY]
Anycast is the network technology that makes GCP's Global Load Balancer faster and more resilient than regional alternatives.
insight: Anycast is the reason Google Search and YouTube load so fast everywhere on Earth.

title: Backend Services (LB Config)
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Configure the destination and capacity for load-balanced traffic.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
The Backend Service is the LB's 'Brain'. It manages: 1. Destinations (Instance Groups or GCS Buckets). 2. Capacity (how much traffic each group can take). 3. Health Checks (checking if backends are alive). 4. Session Affinity (sending a user back to the same VM).

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud compute backend-services list --global` # List all global backends
* `gcloud compute backend-services get-health [NAME] --global` # Check backend health

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
A web admin configures a Backend Service with 'Session Affinity' for a legacy shopping cart app that stores user data in the VM's local memory instead of a database.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Setting the 'Capacity' too high, causing the LB to keep sending traffic to a VM that is already overloaded and crashing.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Use Network Endpoint Groups (NEGs) as your backends if you are load balancing to containers (GKE) or serverless (Cloud Run) for better integration.

[SUMMARY]
Backend Services define the intelligence behind how the Load Balancer chooses and monitors its target resources.
insight: Session Affinity is useful for legacy apps that store user data in the VM's local RAM.

title: SSL Termination (HTTPS)
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Secure your web traffic by managing SSL certificates centrally at the Load Balancer.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
You don't have to manage certs on every VM. The Global LB handles 'SSL Termination': it decrypts incoming HTTPS traffic from the user and sends plain HTTP to your internal VMs over Google's secure backbone. Google-managed certs are free and auto-renewed.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud compute ssl-certificates list` # View all certificates
* `gcloud compute ssl-certificates describe [NAME]` # Check expiration dates

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
An IT team switches from expensive, manually-managed SSL certs to free 'Google-managed certificates', eliminating the risk of a website outage caused by an expired cert.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Using self-signed certificates for production. Browsers will show a 'Not Secure' warning. Always use Google-managed or valid CA-signed certificates.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Enable 'SSL Policy: Modern' on your load balancer frontend to disable old, insecure encryption protocols and protect your users.

[SUMMARY]
Centralized SSL management at the load balancer level improves security and drastically reduces operational overhead.
insight: Using Google-managed certificates is the #1 way to reduce operational overhead for web apps.

title: URL Maps (Path Routing)
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Implement content-based routing to direct traffic to different GCP services.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
URL Maps allow you to route based on the path or host. Example: `mysite.com/video/*` goes to a VM cluster, while `mysite.com/images/*` goes to a Cloud Storage bucket. This is the core of a 'Microservices' architecture.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud compute url-maps describe [NAME]` # View path-based routing rules
* `gcloud compute url-maps list` # List all routing maps

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
A media company uses a single domain. Their URL Map sends `/app` traffic to a GKE cluster and `/static` traffic to a GCS bucket to save on compute costs.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Forgetting to set a 'Default Service'. If a user visits a path that isn't in your map, the LB needs a default destination to send them to.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Use URL Maps to perform 'HTTP to HTTPS' redirection automatically at the load balancer level for a better user experience.

[SUMMARY]
URL Maps provide the high-level routing logic that allows a single IP address to power multiple disparate cloud services.
insight: URL Maps also allow you to perform 'URL Redirects' (e.g., HTTP to HTTPS) at the load balancer level.

title: Peering vs. Shared VPC (Exam Guide)
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Choose the correct multi-project networking strategy for the Associate Cloud Engineer exam.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
PEERING: For connecting independent projects (even in different Orgs). Decentralized management. SHARED VPC: For multiple projects within the same company. One 'Host' project manages the network for 'Service' projects. Centralized management.

[COMMANDS]
* `echo 'Peering = Equal Partners | Shared VPC = Parent-Child'` # (Conceptual logic)

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
A central IT department uses Shared VPC to control all network subnets, while allowing the 'Marketing' and 'Engineering' teams to manage their own VMs in their own projects.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Using VPC Peering when you need central firewall control. Peering forces each project to maintain its own firewalls; Shared VPC centralizes them in the Host project.

[BEST PRACTICE]
If you see the term 'Host Project' or 'Service Project' on the exam, the answer is ALWAYS Shared VPC.

[SUMMARY]
Shared VPC is for centralized enterprise control; VPC Peering is for connecting independent network islands.
insight: You can combine them! A Host Project in Company A can be peered with a VPC in Company B.

lab.command: echo 'Peering = Equal Partners | Shared VPC = Parent-Child'
lab.output: Peering = Equal Partners | Shared VPC = Parent-Child

title: Alias IP Ranges
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Assign multiple internal IP ranges to a single VM for advanced container networking.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
Alias IP ranges allow a VM to have its primary IP plus additional 'sub-ranges'. This is the foundation of GKE 'VPC-Native' mode, where the VM is the Node, and it uses its Alias range to give every Pod its own routable VPC IP address.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud compute instances describe [VM] --format='get(networkInterfaces[0].aliasIpRanges)'` # View alias ranges

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
In a Kubernetes cluster, a Node VM has a primary IP of `10.0.1.5`, but it also has an Alias Range of `10.1.0.0/24`. Every Pod running on that node gets an IP from that secondary range.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Using 'Overlay' networks in GCP. Alias IPs are natively routable in the VPC, making networking simpler and faster than traditional container overlay systems.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Always use Alias IP ranges (VPC-Native mode) for Kubernetes Engine to ensure your Pod IPs are visible to your firewalls and other VPC resources.

[SUMMARY]
Alias IP ranges enable sophisticated, high-performance networking for containerized workloads in Google Cloud.
insight: Alias IPs are better than traditional 'Overlay' networks because they are visible and routable natively in the VPC.

title: LB Health Checks
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Configure sophisticated health checks to ensure traffic only reaches functional backends.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
Load balancer health checks go beyond simple pings. They can check specific HTTP paths (e.g. /healthz) or ports. You can tune the 'Unhealthy Threshold' (how many failures until a VM is out) and the 'Healthy Threshold' (how many successes to get back in).

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud compute health-checks create http [NAME] --port=80 --request-path=/health` # Create health check
* `gcloud compute health-checks list` # View all checks

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
A developer sets up a health check that queries the database. If the database goes down, the health check fails, and the LB stops sending users to that VM until the DB is fixed.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Setting a very strict threshold (e.g. 1 failure). A temporary network blip or a slow CPU spike could cause the LB to kill all your VMs accidentally.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Always create a dedicated `/health` or `/status` endpoint in your application that only returns 200 OK when all internal components are fully operational.

[SUMMARY]
Health checks are the 'eyes' of the load balancer, ensuring high availability by routing traffic away from failing resources.
insight: If ALL your backends fail health checks, the LB will fail-open and send traffic to all of them as a last resort.

lab.command: gcloud compute health-checks create http web-hc --port=80 --request-path=/health

title: Firewall Priorities (Conflict Resolution)
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Master the ordering of firewall rules to ensure your security policy is correctly applied.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
Rules are evaluated from LOWEST NUMBER (0) to HIGHEST (65535). Once a packet matches a rule, evaluation stops. If you have a 'Deny All' at priority 1000 and an 'Allow My IP' at priority 2000, your IP will be DENIED because the first rule matched first.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud compute firewall-rules describe [NAME] --format='get(priority)'` # Check rule priority
* `gcloud compute firewall-rules update [NAME] --priority=[NEW_NUM]` # Change priority

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
A security admin uses priority 10 to allow traffic from the company VPN and priority 65534 to block all other internet traffic, ensuring the 'Allow' rule always wins.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Leaving all rules at the default priority (1000). This makes it difficult to predict what happens when you have overlapping 'Allow' and 'Deny' logic.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Use a consistent priority scheme: 0-100 for emergency overrides, 1000 for standard app rules, and 60000+ for broad security guardrails.

[SUMMARY]
Rule priority is the definitive 'tie-breaker' in GCP's distributed firewall system.
insight: Implicit rules have priority 65535—literally the last rules in the chain.

title: PSC: Endpoints & Backends
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Differentiate between Endpoint and Backend types of Private Service Connect.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
PSC ENDPOINTS: For consuming Google APIs (Storage, BigQuery) via a private internal IP. PSC BACKENDS: For pointing an HTTP(S) Load Balancer at a service running in a completely different VPC or company without peering.

[COMMANDS]
* `echo 'Endpoints = Internal API access | Backends = Cross-company app access'` # (Logical distinction)

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
A SaaS provider uses PSC Backends to share their application with 100 different customers on GCP without having to peer with 100 different (and overlapping) customer VPCs.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Using PSC when simple Private Google Access would work. If you only need to reach Google APIs from one subnet, Private Google Access is simpler and free.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Use PSC Backends for complex multi-organization architectures where you need to provide a managed service securely and at scale.

[SUMMARY]
Private Service Connect is the most flexible tool for bridging services across organizational and network boundaries in Google Cloud.
insight: Private Service Connect is built on top of the same technology that powers Google's own internal services.

lab.command: echo 'Endpoints = For APIs | Backends = For multi-VPC apps'
lab.output: Endpoints = For APIs | Backends = For multi-VPC apps

title: VPC Network Peering: Routes
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Manage the propagation of custom routes between peered VPC networks.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
When peering VPCs, you must explicitly choose to EXPORT and IMPORT custom routes. Example: if VPC-A has a VPN to your office, and you peer VPC-B with VPC-A, VPC-B can only reach your office if A exports the VPN route and B imports it.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud compute networks peerings update [PEER_NAME] --network=[VPC] --export-custom-routes` # Export routes
* `gcloud compute networks peerings update [PEER_NAME] --network=[VPC] --import-custom-routes` # Import routes

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
A hub-and-spoke network uses route propagation so that all 'Spoke' VPCs can reach the central 'Hub' VPC's shared services and on-premises connection.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Assuming peering automatically shares all routes. By default, only subnet routes are shared; VPN and Interconnect routes must be manually enabled for export/import.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Always verify the routing table in the GCP Console after setting up peering to ensure the expected routes from the peer are actually visible.

[SUMMARY]
Explicit route management is the key to building complex, functional multi-network architectures using VPC Peering.
insight: On the exam: If peering is up but custom VPN routes aren't working, check the 'Import/Export custom routes' flags.

lab.command: gcloud compute networks peerings update peer-ab --network=vpc-a --export-custom-routes

title: Networking Summary
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Recap the essential components of the Google Cloud networking ecosystem.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
You've mastered global VPCs, custom subnets, and stateful firewalls. You understand hybrid connectivity (VPN/Interconnect/NAT) and how to scale globally using HTTP(S) and Network Load Balancers. Finally, you've explored advanced security with Cloud Armor and VPC Service Controls.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud compute networks list` # Final network audit
* `gcloud compute forwarding-rules list` # Check all entry points

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
A Cloud Engineer architected a secure system with a Custom VPC, private VMs using Cloud NAT for updates, and a Global HTTP(S) Load Balancer protected by Cloud Armor WAF rules.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Treating cloud networking like on-prem networking. Always remember the global, software-defined, and distributed nature of GCP services for the ACE exam.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Follow a 'Defense in Depth' strategy: use firewalls, VPC Service Controls, Cloud Armor, and Private Google Access together to secure your data.

[SUMMARY]
Networking is the 'nervous system' of your cloud environment, connecting all compute and storage components into a functional system.
insight: Networking is often the hardest part of the ACE exam. Review VPC Peering vs. Shared VPC one more time!
